3g of salt taken with no water = increases blood osmolalityOsmoreceptors detect this = send signal to hypothalamusInhibited ADH secretion (less water reabsorbed)More water reabsorbed from collecting duct = decreased blood osmolality = decreased GFR  All other options are incorrect as they do not follow the pattern of increase/decrease in the right order. The first option is wrong because it says that ADH levels remain the same when it should be decreasing. The second option is wrong because it states that ADH levels also decreases with the decrease in blood osmolality. The third option is wrong because although it is correct that the blood osmolality decreases and the ADH levels decreases, it does not say what happens to the GFR. The fourth option is correct because it follows the pattern correctly. The fifth option is wrong because although it is correct that the blood osmolality increases, it does not say what happens to the ADH levels or the GFR. It also contradicts itself by saying that the GFR increases when more water is being reabsorbed. This is because less water is being reabsorbed which means that more water leaves the body. Hence, the GFR would increase. However, since less water is being reabsorbed, this means that there is more water leaving the body and hence, the blood osmolality decreases. Since the osmoreceptors detect this, it sends a signal to the hypothalamus which then inhibits the release of ADH. Therefore, ADH levels decrease. These were covered in the lecture 'Regulation of Water Excretion' in PCS 2. I tried to make the multiple choice questions more challenging than just remembering the facts. Erb-duchennes palsy - Erb-Duchenne palsy involves injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus. This condition may also be associated with claw hand and/or fracture of the humerus.Klumpke paralysis - Klumpke paralysis involves injury to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus. A - Loss of proprioception and vibration sensation indicates that this is an upper motor neuron lesion. This could be due to a tumour or syringomyelia. Syringomyelia is a disorder whereby cerebrospinal fluid leaks from the subarachnoid space into the spinal cord. This takes up room within the spinal cord and causes scarring which forms a cyst around the spinal cord called a syrinx. This syrinx then expands and pushes down upon the spinal cord, causing the upper motor neuron signs seen above. The patient would have a normal MRC score as this is not an effector nerve lesion. The patient would have bilateral lower motor neuron signs depending on the level of the lesion. There would also be a loss of pain and temp sensation below the level of the lesion. E - Reduced blood supply to the centre of the spinal cord results in Brown-Sequard syndrome. This is characterised by ipsilateral paralysis, loss of pain and temp sensation and contralateral loss of dorsal column function (vibration and proprioception). Sentinel cells are macrophages, microglia, dendritic cells and Langerhan cells - all cells which have a semi-permanent residence within the tissues of the body. They monitor the environment around them, and present any foreign bodies to the nearby naïve T cells, which are also resident within the tissue. They do not detect viruses directly; it is only when the virus infects a macrophage or another cell that the sentinel cell will detect the antigens produced by the virus.   NK cells are free-roaming cells of the immune system, which travel through the bloodstream and other fluid such as lymph, searching for cancerous or virally-infected cells. Upon finding such a target cell, they release granzymes and perforins, which cause apoptosis of the target cell. This is called 'killing by contact'. NK cells are a vital part of the innate response to viral infection, but they are not resident within tissues, so cannot be considered sentinel cells. These can then be used in a formula to calculate the risk of Down’s Syndrome. The combined test involves measuring these same four markers from maternal serum but only between 11 and 13+6 weeks gestation.
